statement: Let $\mu$ be a measure. The [Lp space](c:lp-space) $L^2(\mu)$ is [complete](c:complete-metric-space). For every [orthonormal set](c:orthonormal-set) $(e_n)_{n \ge 1}$ in $L^2(\mu)$ and all scalars $c_n$ with $\sum_n |c_n|^2 < \infty$, the series $\sum_n c_n e_n$ converges in $L^2(\mu)$ to an $f$ with $\langle f, e_n\rangle = c_n$ for all $n$ and $\|f\|_2^2 = \sum_n |c_n|^2$.

hypotheses.text: $\mu$ is a measure, and $L^2(\mu)$ is the [Lp space](c:lp-space) of its square integrable functions modulo null functions.
$(e_n)_{n \ge 1}$ is an [orthonormal set](c:orthonormal-set) in $L^2(\mu)$.
The scalars $c_n$ satisfy $\sum_n |c_n|^2 < \infty$.

conclusion: $L^2(\mu)$ is complete, and $f = \sum_n c_n e_n$ converges in $L^2(\mu)$ with [Fourier coefficients](c:fourier-coefficients) $\langle f, e_n\rangle = c_n$ and $\|f\|_2^2 = \sum_n |c_n|^2$.

proofs.name: Fast Cauchy subsequence and partial sums
proofs.slogan: Prove that $L^2$ is complete through a fast Cauchy subsequence, then sum the orthonormal series through its Cauchy partial sums.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for real or complex scalars and any measure. A finite orthonormal set is the case $c_n = 0$ for large $n$.

roles.why: The measure gives the integrals on which monotone convergence and Fatou's lemma act.
Orthonormality turns the squared norm of a block of the series into a sum of $|c_n|^2$ and fixes the coefficients.
Square summability makes the tails $\sum_{n > N} |c_n|^2$ small.

steps.slogan: Choose a subsequence of a Cauchy sequence with consecutive distances below $2^{-j}$.
steps.detail: Let $(f_k)$ be a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) in $L^2(\mu)$. Because its tail distances tend to $0$, there are indices $k_1 < k_2 < \dots$ with $\|f_{k_{j+1}} - f_{k_j}\|_2 < 2^{-j}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the subsequence converges [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere) to a function $f$.
steps.detail: Let $g = \sum_j |f_{k_{j+1}} - f_{k_j}|$. Minkowski's inequality and monotone convergence give $\|g\|_2 \le 1$, so $g < \infty$ almost everywhere. There the telescoping series $f_{k_1} + \sum_j (f_{k_{j+1}} - f_{k_j})$ converges absolutely to a limit $f$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit with Fatou's lemma to get convergence in $L^2$.
steps.detail: For fixed $j$, Fatou's lemma gives $\|f - f_{k_j}\|_2 \le \liminf_i \|f_{k_i} - f_{k_j}\|_2 \le 2^{1-j}$, so $f \in L^2(\mu)$ and $f_{k_j} \to f$. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges, so $L^2(\mu)$ is [complete](c:complete-metric-space).

steps.slogan: Show that the partial sums of $\sum_n c_n e_n$ form a Cauchy sequence.
steps.detail: Let $S_N = \sum_{n \le N} c_n e_n$. Orthonormality and the Pythagorean theorem give $\|S_M - S_N\|_2^2 = \sum_{N < n \le M} |c_n|^2$ for $M > N$, and this tends to $0$ because $\sum_n |c_n|^2$ converges.

steps.slogan: Take the limit $f$ of the partial sums and read off its coefficients.
steps.detail: By step 3 the partial sums converge to some $f \in L^2(\mu)$. For $N \ge k$, $\langle S_N, e_k\rangle = c_k$ and $\|S_N\|_2^2 = \sum_{n \le N} |c_n|^2$, so continuity of the inner product and the norm gives $\langle f, e_k\rangle = c_k$ and $\|f\|_2^2 = \sum_n |c_n|^2$.

concepts.c:lp-space: The space whose completeness and series the theorem describes.
concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness gives the limit of the Cauchy partial sums.
concepts.c:orthonormal-set: Orthonormality turns norms of partial sums into sums of squares.
concepts.c:fourier-coefficients: The limit has the prescribed coefficients against the orthonormal set.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Completeness is proved for an arbitrary Cauchy sequence.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: The fast subsequence converges pointwise outside a null set.

source.note: The classical proof of the completeness of L^p and of the Riesz-Fischer theorem, as in W. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, chapters 3 and 4.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) and let $\rho, \sigma$ be [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation) unitary matrix representations of $G$ over $\mathbb{C}$, with $d = \dim\rho$. If $\rho$ and $\sigma$ are inequivalent, then $\sum_{g} \rho_{ij}(g)\overline{\sigma_{kl}(g)} = 0$, and $\sum_{g} \rho_{ij}(g)\overline{\rho_{kl}(g)} = \frac{|G|}{d}\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}$. Hence the irreducible [characters](c:character-of-a-representation) are orthonormal.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
$\rho$ and $\sigma$ are [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation) complex representations of $G$ of degrees $d$ and $d'$.
The matrices $\rho(g)$ and $\sigma(g)$ are [unitary](c:unitary-operator).

conclusion: The average $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g \rho_{ij}(g)\overline{\sigma_{kl}(g)}$ is $0$ for inequivalent $\rho, \sigma$ and $\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}/d$ for $\sigma = \rho$, and $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g \chi_\rho(g)\overline{\chi_\sigma(g)}$ is $0$ or $1$ in the same two cases.

proofs.name: Averaging and Schur's lemma
proofs.slogan: Average a matrix over the group to get an intertwiner, and let Schur's lemma force it to be zero or a scalar.
proofs.scope: Both cases of the relations and the character corollary. For $\sigma$ equivalent but not equal to $\rho$ the coefficient sums depend on the basis, so the statement uses $\sigma = \rho$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the average a finite sum and allows the reindexing.
Irreducibility is what Schur's lemma needs.
Unitarity turns $\sigma(g^{-1})$ into the conjugate transpose, so the entries become the coefficient sums.

steps.slogan: Average an arbitrary matrix $X$ into the map $T_X = \sum_g \rho(g) X \sigma(g^{-1})$.
steps.detail: For any $d \times d'$ matrix $X$ the sum $T_X$ is finite because $G$ is [finite](c:finite-group). Reindexing $g \mapsto hg$ gives $\rho(h) T_X = T_X \sigma(h)$ for every $h \in G$, so $T_X$ intertwines $\sigma$ with $\rho$.

steps.slogan: Force $T_X$ to be zero or a scalar matrix by Schur's lemma.
steps.detail: Because $\rho$ and $\sigma$ are [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation), Schur's lemma gives $T_X = 0$ when they are inequivalent. When $\sigma = \rho$ it gives $T_X = \lambda_X I$, and the [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix) gives $d\,\lambda_X = |G| \operatorname{tr} X$.

steps.slogan: Choose $X = E_{jl}$ and read the entry $(i, k)$ of $T_X$.
steps.detail: Since $\sigma(g)$ is [unitary](c:unitary-operator), $\sigma(g^{-1})_{lk} = \overline{\sigma_{kl}(g)}$, so the $(i, k)$ entry of $T_{E_{jl}}$ is $\sum_g \rho_{ij}(g)\overline{\sigma_{kl}(g)}$. Step 2 makes it $0$ in the inequivalent case and $\frac{|G|}{d}\delta_{jl}\delta_{ik}$ for $\sigma = \rho$, because $\operatorname{tr} E_{jl} = \delta_{jl}$.

steps.slogan: Sum the coefficient relations over $i = j$ and $k = l$ to get the character relations.
steps.detail: Since $\chi_\rho(g) = \sum_i \rho_{ii}(g)$, step 3 gives $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g \chi_\rho(g)\overline{\chi_\sigma(g)} = 0$ for inequivalent $\rho, \sigma$ and $\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i,k} \delta_{ik}\delta_{ik} = 1$ for $\sigma = \rho$.

concepts.c:finite-group: A finite group allows the average over all its elements.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Schur's lemma applies only to irreducible representations.
concepts.c:unitary-operator: Unitary matrices invert by conjugate transposition, giving the coefficient sums.
concepts.c:character-of-a-representation: The character relations are the traces of the coefficient relations.
concepts.c:trace-of-a-matrix: The trace fixes the scalar that Schur's lemma leaves open.

source.note: The standard averaging proof, as in J.-P. Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups, section 2.2.

statement: Let $a$ be a normal element of a unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) $A$ and let $f$ be a complex function [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) $\sigma(a)$. Then the element $f(a)$ given by the [continuous functional calculus](c:continuous-functional-calculus) has spectrum $\sigma(f(a)) = f(\sigma(a))$.

hypotheses.text: $A$ is a unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra).
The element $a \in A$ is normal: $a^*a = aa^*$.
The function $f\colon \sigma(a) \to \mathbb{C}$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).

formal.difference: The declaration holds in any ring with a continuous functional calculus over a scalar ring $R$ for elements that satisfy its predicate, which covers normal elements over $\mathbb{C}$, self-adjoint elements over $\mathbb{R}$ and nonnegative elements over $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. There the spectral property is an axiom of the class, which the C*-algebra instance proves as below.

proofs.name: Gelfand isomorphism and spectral permanence
proofs.slogan: Identify the C*-algebra generated by $a$ with $C(\sigma(a))$, where spectra are ranges, and keep spectra under the inclusion into $A$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for normal elements of unital C*-algebras. For $A = 0$ both sides are empty.

roles.why: The C*-identity gives real spectra of self-adjoint elements and the Gelfand-Naimark isomorphism.
Normality makes the subalgebra generated by $a$ commutative.
Continuity puts $f$ in $C(\sigma(a))$, the domain of the calculus.

steps.slogan: Form the C*-subalgebra $B$ generated by $1$ and $a$.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be the closure in $A$ of the polynomials in $a$ and $a^*$. Because $a$ is normal, $a$ and $a^*$ commute, so $B$ is a commutative unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra).

steps.slogan: Show that each element of $B$ has the same spectrum in $B$ and in $A$.
steps.detail: For self-adjoint $h \in B$, $\sigma_B(h)$ is real, so it equals its boundary, which lies in $\sigma_A(h)$; hence $\sigma_B(h) = \sigma_A(h)$. If $b \in B$ is invertible in $A$, this for $h = b^*b$ gives $(b^*b)^{-1} \in B$, and then $b^{-1} = (b^*b)^{-1}b^* \in B$.

steps.slogan: Identify $B$ with $C(\sigma(a))$ through the Gelfand transform.
steps.detail: The Gelfand-Naimark theorem gives an isometric *-isomorphism of $B$ with $C(\Delta)$, where $\Delta$ is the [character space](c:gelfand-spectrum) of $B$. The map $\varphi \mapsto \varphi(a)$ is a homeomorphism of $\Delta$ onto $\sigma_B(a) = \sigma(a)$, so the inverse $\Phi\colon C(\sigma(a)) \to B$ sends the identity function to $a$, and $f(a) = \Phi(f)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the spectrum of a function in $C(\sigma(a))$ is its range.
steps.detail: On the compact set $\sigma(a)$, the [continuous](c:continuous-function) function $f - \lambda$ has a continuous inverse exactly when $f$ never takes the value $\lambda$. So the spectrum of $f$ in $C(\sigma(a))$ is $f(\sigma(a))$.

steps.slogan: Chain the equal spectra through $\Phi$ and the inclusion $B \subseteq A$.
steps.detail: A *-isomorphism keeps invertibility, so $\sigma_B(\Phi(f))$ is the spectrum of $f$ in $C(\sigma(a))$. With steps 2 and 4, $\sigma_A(f(a)) = \sigma_B(\Phi(f)) = f(\sigma(a))$.

concepts.c:c-star-algebra: The C*-identity drives both the Gelfand isomorphism and spectral permanence.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuous functions on $\sigma(a)$ form the domain of the calculus.
concepts.c:spectrum-of-an-operator: The theorem compares two spectra, before and after applying $f$.
concepts.c:continuous-functional-calculus: The calculus defines $f(a)$ as the image of $f$ under $\Phi$.
concepts.c:gelfand-spectrum: The character space of $B$ is homeomorphic to $\sigma(a)$.

source.note: mathlib rewrites with cfcHom_map_spectrum, an axiom of ContinuousFunctionalCalculus; the instance IsStarNormal.instContinuousFunctionalCalculus proves it by StarSubalgebra.spectrum_eq, AlgEquiv.spectrum_eq and ContinuousMap.spectrum_eq_range.

statement: In a quantum field theory that satisfies the [Wightman axioms](c:wightman-axioms), let $\varphi$ be a field that transforms under the irreducible representation $D^{(j,k)}$ of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, the covering group of the [Lorentz group](c:lorentz-group). If $j + k$ is an integer and $\varphi$ anticommutes with $\varphi^*$ at spacelike separation, or $j + k$ is a half-integer and they commute there, then $\varphi = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The fields satisfy the [Wightman axioms](c:wightman-axioms): Poincaré covariance, the spectral condition, locality and a unique cyclic vacuum $\Omega$.
$\varphi$ transforms under the irreducible representation $D^{(j,k)}$ of $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$, the covering group of the [Lorentz group](c:lorentz-group).

$\varphi$ has the wrong statistics: $\varphi(x)$ and $\varphi^*(y)$ anticommute for spacelike $x - y$ when $j + k$ is an integer, and commute when $j + k$ is a half-integer ([spinor](c:spinor) fields).

conclusion: $\varphi = 0$; so nonzero fields of integer spin are bosons and nonzero fields of half-integer spin are fermions.

proofs.name: Analytic continuation of two-point functions
proofs.slogan: Continue the two-point functions analytically, relate the two orders by the complex Lorentz inversion $-1$, and conclude that the field kills the vacuum.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the analyticity, the complex Lorentz covariance and the Reeh-Schlieder step rest on the cited work. Only the two-point functions of $\varphi$ and $\varphi^*$ enter.

roles.why: The spectral condition gives analyticity, covariance gives the complex Lorentz group, and locality with a cyclic vacuum gives Reeh-Schlieder.
The representation $D^{(j,k)}$ fixes the sign $(-1)^{2(j+k)}$ that the inversion $-1$ produces.
The assumed commutation relation has the opposite sign at spacelike points.

steps.slogan: Continue the two-point functions analytically into the forward and backward tubes.
steps.detail: The spectral condition makes $\langle\Omega, \varphi(x)\varphi^*(y)\Omega\rangle$ and $\langle\Omega, \varphi^*(y)\varphi(x)\Omega\rangle$ boundary values of holomorphic functions of $x - y$ in tubes. The cited work proves this [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) from the support of the Fourier transforms of the Wightman distributions.

steps.slogan: Relate the two orderings at real spacelike points by the complex Lorentz inversion $-1$.
steps.detail: By the Bargmann-Hall-Wightman theorem the continued functions are covariant under the proper complex [Lorentz group](c:lorentz-group), which contains $-1$. At real spacelike (Jost) points this gives $\langle\varphi(x)\varphi^*(y)\rangle = (-1)^{2(j+k)}\langle\varphi^*(y)\varphi(x)\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Combine this relation with the wrong statistics to make both two-point functions vanish.
steps.detail: The assumed relation gives the same identity with the opposite sign, so both expectation values vanish at spacelike separation. The Jost points form a real open set, so the holomorphic functions vanish identically, and both two-point functions vanish for all $x, y$.

steps.slogan: Smear the fields to show that $\varphi(f)$ and $\varphi(f)^*$ annihilate the vacuum.
steps.detail: For a test function $f$, $\|\varphi(f)^*\Omega\|^2 = \langle\Omega, \varphi(f)\varphi(f)^*\Omega\rangle = 0$ by step 3. In the same way $\|\varphi(f)\Omega\|^2 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude $\varphi = 0$ from the Reeh-Schlieder theorem.
steps.detail: By the Reeh-Schlieder theorem the vacuum is cyclic for fields in the spacelike complement of the support of $f$. These fields commute or anticommute with $\varphi(f)$, so $\varphi(f)\Omega = 0$ makes $\varphi(f)$ vanish on a dense set, and $\varphi(f) = 0$.

concepts.c:wightman-axioms: The axioms supply analyticity, covariance, locality and the vacuum.
concepts.c:lorentz-group: The complex Lorentz group contains the inversion that relates the two orders.
concepts.c:spinor: Spinor fields carry half-integer spin and the sign $-1$ under inversion.
concepts.c:analytic-continuation: Holomorphy carries the vanishing from Jost points to all points.

source.ref: R. F. Streater and A. S. Wightman, PCT, Spin and Statistics, and All That, W. A. Benjamin, New York, 1964; reprinted by Princeton University Press, 2000, chapter 4
source.note: Streater and Wightman prove the theorem of Burgoyne and of Lüders and Zumino (1958) from the analyticity of Wightman functions, the Bargmann-Hall-Wightman theorem and the Reeh-Schlieder theorem.

statement: The category of [Boolean algebras](c:boolean-algebra) and homomorphisms is [dually equivalent](c:duality-of-categories) to the category of [Stone spaces](c:stone-space) (compact Hausdorff totally disconnected spaces) and continuous maps. The duality sends an algebra $B$ to the space $S(B)$ of its [ultrafilters](c:ultrafilter) and a space $X$ to the algebra of its [clopen](c:clopen-subset) sets.

hypotheses.text: The morphisms of [Boolean algebras](c:boolean-algebra) are the maps that keep $0$, $1$, meet, join and complement.
A [Stone space](c:stone-space) is a compact Hausdorff, totally disconnected space, and its morphisms are continuous maps.

conclusion: The contravariant functors $S$ and $\mathrm{Clop}$ come with natural isomorphisms $B \cong \mathrm{Clop}(S(B))$ and $X \cong S(\mathrm{Clop}(X))$.

proofs.name: Ultrafilter space and clopen algebra
proofs.slogan: Topologize the ultrafilters of $B$ by the sets $U_a$, show that both round trips are isomorphisms, and check naturality.
proofs.scope: The duality between all Boolean algebras and all Stone spaces, with the Boolean prime ideal theorem from the axiom of choice. The trivial algebra corresponds to the empty space.

roles.why: The Boolean operations make each $U_a$ clopen and make ultrafilters prime.
Compactness, the Hausdorff property and total disconnectedness let clopen sets separate and reach every point.

steps.slogan: Topologize the ultrafilters of $B$ and show that $S(B)$ is a Stone space.
steps.detail: Give $S(B)$ the topology with basic sets $U_a = \{p : a \in p\}$; each $U_a$ is [clopen](c:clopen-subset) because its complement is $U_{\neg a}$. Ultrafilters are the homomorphisms $B \to \{0, 1\}$, a closed subspace of the compact Hausdorff space $\{0, 1\}^B$ by Tychonoff's theorem, and a clopen basis makes it totally disconnected.

steps.slogan: Show that $a \mapsto U_a$ is an isomorphism of $B$ onto $\mathrm{Clop}(S(B))$.
steps.detail: The map keeps the operations because [ultrafilters](c:ultrafilter) are prime, and it is injective because each $a \ne 0$ lies in an ultrafilter by the Boolean prime ideal theorem. A clopen set is compact and open, so it is a finite union $U_{a_1} \cup \dots \cup U_{a_n} = U_{a_1 \vee \dots \vee a_n}$.

steps.slogan: Show that each point $x$ and its clopen neighborhoods give a homeomorphism $X \to S(\mathrm{Clop}(X))$.
steps.detail: The clopen sets that contain $x$ form an ultrafilter, and clopen sets separate the points of a compact Hausdorff totally disconnected space, so the map is injective. By compactness every ultrafilter of clopen sets has a common point, so the map is onto, and a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.

steps.slogan: Define the functors on morphisms and check that both isomorphisms are natural.
steps.detail: A homomorphism $h\colon B \to C$ gives the continuous map $p \mapsto h^{-1}(p)$, since the preimage of $U_a$ is $U_{h(a)}$, and a continuous map $f$ gives the homomorphism $K \mapsto f^{-1}(K)$. Both reverse composition, and the maps of steps 2 and 3 commute with them, so they form a [duality](c:duality-of-categories).

concepts.c:boolean-algebra: Boolean algebras are the algebraic side of the duality.
concepts.c:duality-of-categories: The two functors reverse arrows and invert each other up to isomorphism.
concepts.c:stone-space: Stone spaces are the topological side of the duality.
concepts.c:ultrafilter: Ultrafilters are the points of the dual space.
concepts.c:clopen-subset: Clopen sets are the elements of the dual algebra.

source.note: The classical proof of M. H. Stone, The theory of representations for Boolean algebras, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 40 (1936), in modern form.

statement: Let $f\colon A \to B$ be a [function](c:function) between [finite sets](c:finite-set) and $n$ a natural number with $|B| \cdot n < |A|$. Then some $y \in B$ has a [fiber](c:fiber) with more than $n$ elements: $|f^{-1}(y)| > n$.

hypotheses.text: $A$ and $B$ are [finite sets](c:finite-set) and $f\colon A \to B$ is a [function](c:function).
The sizes satisfy $|B| \cdot n < |A|$.

proofs.name: Sum of the fiber sizes
proofs.slogan: Count $A$ as the sum of the fiber sizes and compare this sum with $|B| \cdot n$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; $n = 1$ is the ordinary pigeonhole principle. If $B$ is empty, then $A$ is empty and the hypothesis $0 < |A|$ fails, so the claim holds vacuously.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the sizes natural numbers and the fiber sum finite.
The strict inequality is what the fiber sum must beat.

steps.slogan: Split $A$ into the fibers $f^{-1}(y)$ for $y \in B$.
steps.detail: Every $x \in A$ lies in exactly one [fiber](c:fiber), namely $f^{-1}(f(x))$, so the fibers are disjoint and cover $A$. Hence $|A| = \sum_{y \in B} |f^{-1}(y)|$.

steps.slogan: Compare the fiber sum with the constant sum $\sum_{y \in B} n = |B| \cdot n$.
steps.detail: The hypothesis and step 1 give $\sum_{y \in B} n = |B| \cdot n < |A| = \sum_{y \in B} |f^{-1}(y)|$.

steps.slogan: Find a term where the fiber sum beats the constant sum.
steps.detail: If $|f^{-1}(y)| \le n$ held for every $y \in B$, summing would give $\sum_{y} |f^{-1}(y)| \le |B| \cdot n$, against step 2. So some $y \in B$ has $|f^{-1}(y)| > n$.

concepts.c:function: The function sorts the elements of $A$ into the boxes of $B$.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finite sets have sizes that add up over a partition.
concepts.c:fiber: The fibers partition $A$, and one of them must be large.

source.note: mathlib applies exists_lt_card_fiber_of_nsmul_lt_card, which sums over fibers with Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to and then uses Finset.exists_lt_of_sum_lt.

statement: Let $\varphi_e$ be the [partial computable function](c:partial-computable-function) with code $e$ in a standard [Gödel numbering](c:godel-numbering) of programs, and let $\langle x, y\rangle$ be the Cantor pairing. There is a total [computable function](c:computable-function) $s$, even primitive recursive, with $\varphi_{s(e, x)}(y) \simeq \varphi_e(\langle x, y\rangle)$ for all $e, x, y$.

hypotheses.text: Programs are the codes of partial recursive functions, built by the constructors zero, succ, left, right, pair, comp, prec and rfind and numbered by a [Gödel numbering](c:godel-numbering).
$\langle x, y\rangle$ is the Cantor pairing, a bijection $\mathbb{N}^2 \to \mathbb{N}$ with computable projections.

conclusion: A primitive recursive $s$ satisfies $\varphi_{s(e, x)}(y) \simeq \varphi_e(\langle x, y\rangle)$ for all $e, x, y$, where both sides are undefined together.

formal.difference: The declaration works with the inductive type Code instead of code numbers and states that $s$ is computable as a map $\mathrm{Code} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Code}$. Forms with $m$ fixed and $n$ free arguments follow by iterated pairing.

proofs.name: Currying by composition
proofs.slogan: Compose the program $e$ with a program that pairs the constant $x$ with the input.
proofs.scope: One fixed and one free argument; tuples of $m$ and $n$ arguments reduce to this case by iterated pairing.

roles.why: The constructors comp and pair, with primitive recursive encodings, build and track the code $s(e, x)$.
The pairing makes $\mathrm{pair}(\mathrm{left}, \mathrm{right})$ the identity and forms the input $\langle x, y\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Build a code $\mathrm{const}(x)$ for the constant function with value $x$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathrm{const}(0)$ be the code zero and $\mathrm{const}(x + 1) = \mathrm{comp}(\mathrm{succ}, \mathrm{const}(x))$. By induction on $x$ this code computes the constant $x$, and $x \mapsto \mathrm{const}(x)$ is primitive recursive.

steps.slogan: Define $s(e, x)$ as $e$ composed with the pair of $\mathrm{const}(x)$ and the identity.
steps.detail: Let $\mathrm{id} = \mathrm{pair}(\mathrm{left}, \mathrm{right})$, which computes $y \mapsto y$ because $\langle \mathrm{left}(y), \mathrm{right}(y)\rangle = y$. Set $s(e, x) = \mathrm{comp}(e, \mathrm{pair}(\mathrm{const}(x), \mathrm{id}))$.

steps.slogan: Show that $s$ is primitive recursive on code numbers.
steps.detail: The encodings of comp and pair are primitive recursive operations on code numbers, and $\mathrm{const}$ is primitive recursive by step 1. Their composite $s$ is primitive recursive, so it is a total [computable function](c:computable-function).

steps.slogan: Evaluate the composed code on an input $y$ and compare with $e$.
steps.detail: The code $\mathrm{pair}(\mathrm{const}(x), \mathrm{id})$ sends $y$ to $\langle x, y\rangle$, and composition runs $e$ on it, so $\varphi_{s(e, x)}(y) \simeq \varphi_e(\langle x, y\rangle)$. With step 3, $s$ is a total computable function with the required property.

concepts.c:partial-computable-function: The theorem specializes the first argument of a partial computable function.
concepts.c:godel-numbering: Codes are numbers, so $s$ is a function on numbers.
concepts.c:computable-function: The specializing map $s$ is total and computable.

source.note: mathlib takes curry c n = comp c (pair (Code.const n) Code.id), proves eval_curry by unfolding the semantics, and gets computability from primrec₂_curry.

statement: Let $C$ be a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) of [free abelian groups](c:free-abelian-group) and $G$ an abelian group. Then [homology](c:homology) and [cohomology](c:cohomology) with coefficients in $G$ fit into natural split [exact sequences](c:exact-sequence) $0 \to H_n(C) \otimes G \to H_n(C \otimes G) \to \mathrm{Tor}(H_{n-1}(C), G) \to 0$ and $0 \to \mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1}(C), G) \to H^n(\mathrm{Hom}(C, G)) \to \mathrm{Hom}(H_n(C), G) \to 0$, with [Tor](c:tor-functor) and [Ext](c:ext-functor) over $\mathbb{Z}$.

hypotheses.text: $C$ is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) of abelian groups with boundary maps $\partial_n\colon C_n \to C_{n-1}$.
Each $C_n$ is a [free abelian group](c:free-abelian-group), as for singular chains.

conclusion: Both sequences are exact and natural in $C$ and $G$, and they split, though not naturally.

proofs.name: Splitting cycles and boundaries
proofs.slogan: Split each chain group into cycles and boundaries, apply $\mathrm{Hom}(-, G)$, and read the long exact sequence through the free resolutions of homology.
proofs.scope: The steps treat cohomology; homology is the same argument with $- \otimes G$ in place of $\mathrm{Hom}(-, G)$ and Tor in place of Ext. Singular (co)homology of a space is the case of singular chains.

roles.why: The boundary maps define the cycles, the boundaries and the homology.
Freeness of $C_{n-1}$ makes $B_{n-1}$ free, so the sequences split and $0 \to B_k \to Z_k \to H_k \to 0$ is a free resolution.

steps.slogan: Split the sequence $0 \to Z_n \to C_n \to B_{n-1} \to 0$ of cycles and boundaries.
steps.detail: Here $Z_n = \ker\partial_n$ and $B_{n-1} = \operatorname{im}\partial_n \subseteq C_{n-1}$. A subgroup of a [free abelian group](c:free-abelian-group) is free, so $B_{n-1}$ is free and the sequence splits.

steps.slogan: Dualize the split sequences into a short exact sequence of cochain complexes.
steps.detail: Regard $Z$ and $B$ as complexes with zero boundary maps. Split sequences stay exact under $\mathrm{Hom}(-, G)$, so $0 \to \mathrm{Hom}(B_{\bullet - 1}, G) \to \mathrm{Hom}(C, G) \to \mathrm{Hom}(Z, G) \to 0$ is a short [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) of cochain complexes.

steps.slogan: Write the long exact [cohomology](c:cohomology) sequence and identify its connecting maps.
steps.detail: Zero differentials make the outer complexes their own cohomology, so the sequence reads $\mathrm{Hom}(Z_{n-1}, G) \to \mathrm{Hom}(B_{n-1}, G) \to H^n(C; G) \to \mathrm{Hom}(Z_n, G) \to \mathrm{Hom}(B_n, G)$. A diagram chase shows that the connecting maps are the duals $i^*$ of the inclusions $i\colon B_k \to Z_k$.

steps.slogan: Read the kernel and cokernel of $i^*$ from the free resolution $0 \to B_k \to Z_k \to H_k \to 0$.
steps.detail: Since $B_k$ and $Z_k$ are free, this sequence is a free resolution of $H_k(C)$. So the kernel of $i^*$ on $\mathrm{Hom}(Z_n, G)$ is $\mathrm{Hom}(H_n(C), G)$, and the cokernel of $i^*$ into $\mathrm{Hom}(B_{n-1}, G)$ is $\mathrm{Ext}(H_{n-1}(C), G)$ by the definition of [Ext](c:ext-functor).

steps.slogan: Cut the long exact sequence at $H^n(C; G)$ and split the short sequence.
steps.detail: Exactness at $H^n(C; G)$ gives $0 \to \operatorname{coker} i^* \to H^n(C; G) \to \ker i^* \to 0$, which is the claimed sequence by step 4, natural because every map comes from $C$ and $G$. A retraction $C_n \to Z_n$ from step 1 extends homomorphisms $Z_n \to G$ to cocycles and splits it, but it depends on that choice.

concepts.c:chain-complex: The theorem starts from a chain complex and its boundary maps.
concepts.c:free-abelian-group: Freeness makes boundaries free, so the chain sequences split.
concepts.c:homology: Integral homology determines the groups with any coefficients.
concepts.c:cohomology: The long exact cohomology sequence carries the computation.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: The theorem and its proof are statements about exact sequences.
concepts.c:tor-functor: Tor measures the failure of homology to commute with tensoring.
concepts.c:ext-functor: Ext is the cokernel that the free resolution produces.

source.note: The proof in A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, theorem 3.2 for cohomology and theorem 3A.3 for homology.

statement: Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ be a [probability space](c:probability-measure), $\mathcal{A}$ a [π-system](c:pi-system) of events, and $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{A})$ a [σ-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) such that every event of $\mathcal{T}$ is [independent](c:independence) of every event of $\mathcal{A}$. Then $P(T) \in \{0, 1\}$ for every $T \in \mathcal{T}$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal{A}$ is a [π-system](c:pi-system): it is closed under finite intersections.
$\mathcal{T}$ is a [σ-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) contained in the σ-algebra $\sigma(\mathcal{A})$ that $\mathcal{A}$ generates.
$P(T \cap A) = P(T)P(A)$ for all $T \in \mathcal{T}$ and $A \in \mathcal{A}$.

proofs.name: Self-independence by the π-λ theorem
proofs.slogan: Extend the independence from the π-system to the generated σ-algebra, then test each event against itself.
proofs.scope: The record names a family of zero-one laws; this is the abstract law behind them. Kolmogorov's law is the case where $\mathcal{A}$ is the union of $\sigma(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ over $n$ for independent $X_k$ and $\mathcal{T}$ is the [tail σ-algebra](c:tail-sigma-algebra).

roles.why: Closure under intersections is what Dynkin's theorem needs.
The inclusion puts $T$ itself among the events independent of $T$.
Independence from $\mathcal{A}$ puts $\mathcal{A}$ inside the class $\mathcal{D}$.

steps.slogan: Fix $T \in \mathcal{T}$ and collect the events independent of $T$ into a class $\mathcal{D}$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{D} = \{B \in \mathcal{F} : P(T \cap B) = P(T)P(B)\}$. It contains $\Omega$, it is closed under complements since $P(T \cap B^c) = P(T) - P(T \cap B)$, and countable additivity closes it under countable disjoint unions. So $\mathcal{D}$ is a [Dynkin system](c:dynkin-system).

steps.slogan: Extend the independence from $\mathcal{A}$ to $\sigma(\mathcal{A})$ by Dynkin's theorem.
steps.detail: The hypothesis gives $\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{D}$. Because $\mathcal{A}$ is a [π-system](c:pi-system), Dynkin's π-λ theorem gives $\sigma(\mathcal{A}) \subseteq \mathcal{D}$.

steps.slogan: Test the event $T$ against itself.
steps.detail: Since $T \in \mathcal{T} \subseteq \sigma(\mathcal{A}) \subseteq \mathcal{D}$, the event $T$ is [independent](c:independence) of itself, so $P(T) = P(T \cap T) = P(T)^2$.

steps.slogan: Solve the equation $p = p^2$ to get $P(T) \in \{0, 1\}$.
steps.detail: The equation $p(1 - p) = 0$ has only the solutions $p = 0$ and $p = 1$, so $P(T)$ is $0$ or $1$.

concepts.c:probability-measure: Additivity of the probability makes $\mathcal{D}$ a Dynkin system.
concepts.c:pi-system: A π-system generates its σ-algebra through Dynkin systems.
concepts.c:sigma-algebra: The σ-algebra $\mathcal{T}$ lies inside the generated σ-algebra.
concepts.c:independence: An event independent of itself has probability 0 or 1.
concepts.c:tail-sigma-algebra: Tail events are the main application, in Kolmogorov's law.
concepts.c:dynkin-system: The events independent of $T$ form a Dynkin system.

source.note: The standard proof of Kolmogorov's zero-one law through Dynkin's π-λ theorem, as in D. Williams, Probability with Martingales, chapter 4.

statement: Let $n \ge 1$. Among any $2n - 1$ integers $a_1, \dots, a_{2n-1}$, with repetitions allowed, some $n$ terms with distinct indices have a sum divisible by $n$; that is, the sum is $0$ in the [modular arithmetic](c:modular-arithmetic) of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.

hypotheses.text: $n$ is a positive integer.
The sequence has at least $2n - 1$ terms.

conclusion: Some set $S$ of exactly $n$ indices has $\sum_{i \in S} a_i \equiv 0 \pmod n$.

formal.difference: The declaration takes the terms in $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$, indexed by a finite set with at least $2n - 1$ elements. It also covers $n = 0$, where $2n - 1$ truncates to $0$ and the empty set works.

proofs.name: Chevalley-Warning and multiplicativity
proofs.slogan: Prove the prime case with the Chevalley-Warning theorem, then pass from $m$ and $k$ to $mk$ by grouping terms into blocks.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 1$ by induction on the number of prime factors; $n = 1$ takes any single term. Extra terms beyond $2n - 1$ are ignored.

roles.why: A positive $n$ is $1$, a prime or a product of smaller factors, which drives the induction.
$2p - 1$ variables beat the degree $2p - 2$, and $2mk - 1$ terms leave room for $2k - 1$ blocks.

steps.slogan: Form two polynomials of degree $p - 1$ in $2p - 1$ variables over $\mathbb{F}_p$.
steps.detail: For a [prime](c:prime-number) $p$ and terms $a_1, \dots, a_{2p-1}$, let $f_1 = \sum_i x_i^{p-1}$ and $f_2 = \sum_i a_i x_i^{p-1}$ over the [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_p$. Their degrees add up to $2p - 2$, less than the number $2p - 1$ of variables.

steps.slogan: Find a nonzero common zero by the Chevalley-Warning theorem.
steps.detail: The Chevalley-Warning theorem makes the number of common zeros of $f_1$ and $f_2$ divisible by $p$. The zero vector is one of them, so there are at least $p \ge 2$, and some common zero $x$ is nonzero.

steps.slogan: Read the required $p$ terms from the support of the nonzero common zero.
steps.detail: By Fermat's little theorem $x_i^{p-1}$ is $1$ on the support $S$ of $x$ and $0$ elsewhere. So $f_1(x) = 0$ gives $p \mid |S|$, and $1 \le |S| \le 2p - 1$ forces $|S| = p$; then $f_2(x) = 0$ gives $\sum_{i \in S} a_i \equiv 0 \pmod p$.

steps.slogan: Extract $2k - 1$ disjoint blocks of size $m$ whose sums are divisible by $m$.
steps.detail: Let $n = mk$ with the theorem known for $m$ and for $k$. After $j \le 2k - 2$ blocks are taken, $(2mk - 1) - jm \ge 2m - 1$ terms remain, so the case $m$ gives one more block. Write the block sums as $m b_1, \dots, m b_{2k-1}$.

steps.slogan: Choose $k$ blocks whose quotients $b_j$ have a sum divisible by $k$.
steps.detail: The case $k$ applied to $b_1, \dots, b_{2k-1}$ gives $k$ blocks with $k \mid \sum b_j$; their union has $mk = n$ terms with sum $m\sum b_j$, divisible by $mk$. Induction on the number of prime factors, with the prime case of step 3, gives every $n \ge 1$.

concepts.c:prime-number: The base case of the induction is a prime modulus.
concepts.c:finite-field: Chevalley-Warning counts zeros of polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_p$.

source.note: mathlib reduces to Int.erdos_ginzburg_ziv, which inducts with Nat.prime_composite_induction; the prime case applies char_dvd_card_solutions_of_add_lt (Chevalley-Warning) to the two polynomials, and the composite case groups disjoint blocks.

statement: Let $T$ satisfy the [divide and conquer](c:divide-and-conquer) [recurrence relation](c:recurrence-relation) $T(n) = g(n) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i T(r_i(n))$ for $n \ge n_0$, with $T > 0$ below $n_0$, $a_i > 0$, $0 < b_i < 1$, $r_i(n) = b_i n + o(n/\log^2 n)$, and $g \ge 0$ of polynomial growth. If $\sum_i a_i b_i^p = 1$, then, in [asymptotic notation](c:asymptotic-notation), $T(n) = \Theta\big(n^p(1 + \int_1^n g(u)u^{-p-1}\,du)\big)$.

hypotheses.text: $T\colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $T(n) = g(n) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i T(r_i(n))$ for $n \ge n_0$, with $r_i(n) < n$ there and $T(n) > 0$ for $n < n_0$.
The constants satisfy $a_i > 0$ and $0 < b_i < 1$, and $r_i(n) - b_i n = o(n/\log^2 n)$.
The function $g$ is nonnegative and grows polynomially: for each $b \in (0, 1)$ there are $c_1, c_2 > 0$ with $c_1 g(n) \le g(u) \le c_2 g(n)$ for $u \in [bn, n]$ and large $n$.

conclusion: $T(n) = \Theta\big(n^p(1 + \int_1^n g(u)u^{-p-1}\,du)\big)$, where $p$ is the unique real number with $\sum_i a_i b_i^p = 1$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the upper bound $T = O(\cdot)$; the lower bound is isBigO_symm_asympBound and the $\Theta$ form is isTheta_asympBound. It uses the sum $\sum_{u < n} g(u)/u^{p+1}$ in place of the integral, which has the same order under polynomial growth.

proofs.name: Smoothed induction
proofs.slogan: Show by strong induction that $T(n) \le C(1 - 1/\log n)B(n)$, using that the bound $B$ nearly reproduces itself under the recurrence.
proofs.scope: The upper bound, as in mathlib, with $B(n) = n^p(1 + \sum_{u < n} g(u)/u^{p+1})$ in place of the integral form. The lower bound is the same induction with the factor $1 + 1/\log n$ and reversed inequalities.

roles.why: The recurrence with $r_i(n) < n$ lets the induction pass from smaller sizes to $n$, and positive base values start it.
Positive $a_i$ and $b_i \in (0, 1)$ give a unique $p$, and the small size errors fit inside the smoothing factor.
Polynomial growth makes the sum of $g(u)/u^{p+1}$ over $[r_i(n), n)$ comparable to $g(n)/n^p$.

steps.slogan: Find the unique exponent $p$ with $\sum_i a_i b_i^p = 1$.
steps.detail: The map $q \mapsto \sum_i a_i b_i^q$ is continuous and strictly decreasing because each $b_i < 1$, and it tends to $\infty$ and to $0$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$. The intermediate value theorem gives exactly one $p$.

steps.slogan: Show that the bound gains a multiple of $g(n)$ when the recurrence acts on it.
steps.detail: Polynomial growth gives $c > 0$ with $n^p\sum_{r_i(n) \le u < n} g(u)/u^{p+1} \ge c\,g(n)$ for large $n$. With $\sum_i a_i b_i^p = 1$ this gives $\sum_i a_i b_i^p n^p (1 + \sum_{u < r_i(n)} g(u)/u^{p+1}) \le B(n) - c\,g(n)$.

steps.slogan: Absorb the size errors $r_i(n) - b_i n$ into the factor $1 - 1/\log n$.
steps.detail: Let $\varepsilon(n) = 1/\log n$. A derivative estimate with $r_i(n) = b_i n + o(n/\log^2 n)$ gives $r_i(n)^p(1 - \varepsilon(r_i(n))) \le b_i^p n^p (1 - \varepsilon(n))$ for large $n$, because $\varepsilon(b_i n) - \varepsilon(n)$ has the larger order $1/\log^2 n$.

steps.slogan: Prove $T(n) \le C(1 - \varepsilon(n))B(n)$ by strong induction on $n$.
steps.detail: Choose $C \ge 2/c$ and large enough for the finitely many base values. For large $n$ the recurrence, the induction hypothesis at $r_i(n) < n$, step 3 and step 2 give $T(n) \le g(n) + C(1 - \varepsilon(n))(B(n) - c\,g(n)) \le C(1 - \varepsilon(n))B(n)$, since $1 - \varepsilon(n) \ge 1/2$.

steps.slogan: Drop the smoothing factor $1 - \varepsilon(n)$, which stays below $1$.
steps.detail: For large $n$, $0 < 1 - \varepsilon(n) \le 1$, so step 4 gives $0 < T(n) \le C\,B(n)$ eventually. This is $T = O(B)$ in [asymptotic notation](c:asymptotic-notation).

concepts.c:divide-and-conquer: Such recurrences count the cost of divide-and-conquer algorithms.
concepts.c:recurrence-relation: The induction runs along the recurrence from smaller sizes.
concepts.c:asymptotic-notation: The result is an order of growth, up to constant factors.

source.note: mathlib proves T_isBigO_smoothingFn_mul_asympBound by isBigO_nat_atTop_induction_of_eventually_pos with smoothingFn 1/log n, using rpow_p_mul_one_sub_smoothingFn_le and eventually_atTop_sumTransform_ge, after Leighton's notes on better master theorems.

statement: In a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$, let $M$ be the [midpoint](c:midpoint) of $BC$, so that $AM$ is a [median](c:median-of-a-triangle). Then $AB^2 + AC^2 = 2AM^2 + 2BM^2$.

hypotheses.text: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are points of a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space).
$M$ is the [midpoint](c:midpoint) of $BC$, so $BM = MC = BC/2$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds for any three points of a real inner product affine space, degenerate triangles included, and writes $BM$ as $BC/2$.

new_concepts.name: median of a triangle
new_concepts.reminder: A median joins a vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side.
new_concepts.definition: In a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$, the median from $A$ is the segment $AM$, where $M$ is the [midpoint](c:midpoint) of the side $BC$.

proofs.name: Law of cosines at the midpoint
proofs.slogan: Write the law of cosines at $M$ in the triangles $ABM$ and $ACM$, whose angles at $M$ are supplementary, and add.
proofs.scope: Any three points. The case $B = C$ is step 1; if $A = M$ the cosine terms vanish because $AM = 0$.

roles.why: Distances and angles of a Euclidean space satisfy the law of cosines.
$M$ between $B$ and $C$ makes the angles supplementary, and $BM = MC$ cancels the cosine terms.

steps.slogan: Treat the degenerate case $B = C$ separately.
steps.detail: If $B = C$, then $M = B = C$ and $BM = 0$. Both sides equal $2AB^2$.

steps.slogan: Write the law of cosines in triangles $ABM$ and $ACM$ with angles $\theta$ and $\pi - \theta$.
steps.detail: For $B \ne C$ the [midpoint](c:midpoint) $M$ lies strictly between $B$ and $C$, so $\angle AMB = \theta$ and $\angle AMC = \pi - \theta$. The law of cosines gives $AB^2 = AM^2 + BM^2 - 2\,AM \cdot BM\cos\theta$ and $AC^2 = AM^2 + MC^2 + 2\,AM \cdot MC\cos\theta$.

steps.slogan: Add the two equations and cancel the cosine terms with $BM = MC$.
steps.detail: Since $BM = MC$, the terms $\mp 2\,AM \cdot BM\cos\theta$ cancel, so $AB^2 + AC^2 = 2AM^2 + BM^2 + MC^2 = 2AM^2 + 2BM^2$. This is Stewart's theorem for the [median](c:median-of-a-triangle), and with step 1 it covers all cases.

concepts.c:triangle: The theorem relates the sides of the triangle $ABC$ to a median.
concepts.c:midpoint: The midpoint splits $BC$ into equal halves, which cancels the cosines.
concepts.c:median-of-a-triangle: The median $AM$ is the length that the identity computes.
concepts.c:euclidean-space: Euclidean distances and angles obey the law of cosines.

source.note: mathlib splits off b = c, then applies Stewart's theorem dist_sq_mul_dist_add_dist_sq_mul_dist at the midpoint with angle_midpoint_eq_pi; that lemma is the law of cosines at the straight angle BMC.

proofs.name: Parallelogram law
proofs.slogan: Write the sides as vectors from $A$ and expand the squared norms, which is the parallelogram law.
proofs.scope: Any three points of an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space), degenerate cases included.

roles.why: The Euclidean distance comes from an inner product, so squared lengths expand.
The midpoint is the average $(B + C)/2$, so $M - A = (u + v)/2$.

steps.slogan: Write the sides and the median as vectors in $u = B - A$ and $v = C - A$.
steps.detail: Then $M - A = (u + v)/2$ and $C - B = v - u$. So $AM = \|u + v\|/2$ and $BM = \|v - u\|/2$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\|u + v\|^2$ and $\|u - v\|^2$ with the inner product.
steps.detail: In an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space), $\|u \pm v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 \pm 2\langle u, v\rangle + \|v\|^2$. Adding gives the [parallelogram](c:parallelogram) law $\|u + v\|^2 + \|u - v\|^2 = 2\|u\|^2 + 2\|v\|^2$.

steps.slogan: Substitute the lengths into the parallelogram law and divide by $2$.
steps.detail: With step 1, step 2 reads $4AM^2 + 4BM^2 = 2AB^2 + 2AC^2$. Dividing by $2$ gives $AB^2 + AC^2 = 2AM^2 + 2BM^2$.

concepts.c:triangle: The triangle $ABC$ is spanned by the vectors $u$ and $v$.
concepts.c:midpoint: The midpoint is the average of $B$ and $C$.
concepts.c:median-of-a-triangle: The median is half the diagonal $u + v$ of the parallelogram.
concepts.c:euclidean-space: Euclidean space is an inner product space, so norms expand.
concepts.c:inner-product-space: The inner product expands the squared norms of sums.
concepts.c:parallelogram: The triangle doubles to the parallelogram with sides $u$ and $v$.

source.note: The vector proof by the parallelogram law, standard in linear algebra courses.

statement: A disc of radius $r > 0$ in the Euclidean plane has [area](c:area) $\pi r^2$, where [π](c:pi) is the ratio of the circumference of a [circle](c:circle) to its diameter.

hypotheses.text: The radius satisfies $r > 0$.
The disc is $D_r = \{(x, y) : x^2 + y^2 \le r^2\}$, and its [area](c:area) is its Lebesgue measure.

proofs.name: Trigonometric substitution
proofs.slogan: Integrate the height $2\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}$ of the disc over $[-r, r]$ with the substitution $x = r\sin\theta$.
proofs.scope: All $r > 0$, with $\pi$ first taken as the half period of sine; step 4 shows that it is the ratio of circumference to diameter. For $r = 0$ the disc is a point of area $0$.

roles.why: A positive radius makes $x = r\sin\theta$ a bijection of $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$ onto $[-r, r]$.
The disc is the region between the graphs of $\pm\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}$.

steps.slogan: Write the area as the [integral](c:integral) of the vertical cross-section length.
steps.detail: The vertical line at $x \in [-r, r]$ meets $D_r$ in a segment of length $2\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}$. As the region between two graphs, $\operatorname{area}(D_r) = \int_{-r}^{r} 2\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}\,dx$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $x = r\sin\theta$ for $\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]$.
steps.detail: Then $dx = r\cos\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{r^2 - x^2} = r\cos\theta$, because $\cos\theta \ge 0$ there. The integral becomes $2r^2\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$.

steps.slogan: Check that the half period of sine is the ratio of circumference to diameter.
steps.detail: The curve $\theta \mapsto (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$ for $\theta \in [0, 2\pi]$ traces the [circle](c:circle) once with constant speed $r$. So the circumference is $2\pi r$, and its ratio to the diameter $2r$ is $\pi$.

steps.slogan: Integrate $\cos^2\theta = (1 + \cos 2\theta)/2$ over $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$.
steps.detail: An antiderivative is $\theta/2 + \sin(2\theta)/4$, and $\sin(\pm\pi) = 0$, so the fundamental theorem of calculus gives the value $\pi/2$. Hence $\operatorname{area}(D_r) = 2r^2 \cdot \pi/2 = \pi r^2$, with [π](c:pi) as in step 3.

concepts.c:area: The area of the disc is the quantity being computed.
concepts.c:pi: The integral produces the half period of sine, which is this ratio.
concepts.c:circle: The circle bounds the disc and defines the ratio π.
concepts.c:integral: The area is computed as an integral of cross-section lengths.

source.note: The standard calculus computation; the mathlib Archive proof Theorems100.area_disc integrates the same height with the antiderivative r^2 arcsin(x/r) + x sqrt(r^2 - x^2) instead of the substitution.

proofs.name: Archimedes' polygon squeeze
proofs.slogan: Squeeze the disc between inscribed and circumscribed regular polygons, whose areas are half the perimeter times the apothem.
proofs.scope: All $r > 0$, with the circumference defined as the limit of the perimeters of inscribed polygons. This is the argument of Archimedes in modern form.

roles.why: A positive radius gives nondegenerate polygons whose apothems tend to $r$.
The disc contains each inscribed polygon and lies inside each circumscribed polygon.

steps.slogan: Split a [regular polygon](c:regular-polygon) into $n$ triangles at its center.
steps.detail: A regular $n$-gon with perimeter $P$ and apothem $h$, the distance from the center to a side, splits into $n$ triangles with base $P/n$ and height $h$. So its area is $\frac12 P h$.

steps.slogan: Bound the area of the disc from below by inscribed regular $n$-gons.
steps.detail: The inscribed $n$-gon lies in $D_r$, so $\frac12 p_n h_n \le \operatorname{area}(D_r)$. As $n \to \infty$ the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) of the perimeters $p_n$ is the circumference $2\pi r$, and $h_n = \sqrt{r^2 - (p_n/2n)^2} \to r$, so $\operatorname{area}(D_r) \ge \pi r^2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the area of the disc from above by circumscribed regular $n$-gons.
steps.detail: The circumscribed $n$-gon contains $D_r$ and has apothem $r$, so $\operatorname{area}(D_r) \le \frac12 P_n r$. It is the inscribed polygon scaled by $r/h_n$, so $P_n = p_n r/h_n \to 2\pi r$, and $\operatorname{area}(D_r) \le \pi r^2$.

steps.slogan: Combine the lower and upper bounds into $\operatorname{area}(D_r) = \pi r^2$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $\pi r^2 \le \operatorname{area}(D_r) \le \pi r^2$, so the [area](c:area) of the disc is $\pi r^2$.

concepts.c:area: The disc area is trapped between two polygon areas.
concepts.c:pi: π enters through the circumference $2\pi r$, the limit of perimeters.
concepts.c:circle: The polygons are inscribed in and circumscribed about the circle.
concepts.c:regular-polygon: Regular polygons have area half perimeter times apothem.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: Perimeters and apothems converge as the number of sides grows.

source.note: Archimedes, Measurement of a Circle, proposition 1, in modern form with limits.

statement: Every [simple polygon](c:simple-polygon) with $n \ge 3$ vertices can be guarded by $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$ guards placed at vertices, so that every point of the polygon is seen by a guard along a segment inside the polygon. For every $n \ge 3$ some simple polygon with $n$ vertices needs $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$ guards.

hypotheses.text: $P$ is a [simple polygon](c:simple-polygon): its boundary is a closed polygonal curve without self-intersections.
$P$ has $n \ge 3$ vertices.

conclusion: Some set of at most $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$ vertices sees all of $P$, and the number $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$ cannot be lowered in general.

proofs.name: Fisk's three-coloring
proofs.slogan: Triangulate the polygon, three-color the vertices of the triangulation, and post guards at the smallest color class.
proofs.scope: Sufficiency in steps 1 to 4 and sharpness by comb polygons in step 5. A triangle, $n = 3$, needs one guard at any vertex.

roles.why: A simple polygon has a diagonal, so it can be triangulated.
The $n$ vertices split into three color classes, one of size at most $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$.

steps.slogan: Triangulate the polygon by $n - 3$ diagonals that do not cross.
steps.detail: Take the leftmost vertex $v$ with neighbors $u, w$: either $uw$ is a diagonal, or the vertex inside triangle $uvw$ farthest from $uw$ joins $v$ by a diagonal. Cutting along diagonals and inducting on $n$ gives a [polygon triangulation](c:polygon-triangulation) into $n - 2$ triangles.

steps.slogan: Color the triangulation vertices with three colors so that each triangle gets all three.
steps.detail: For $n \ge 4$ the dual graph of the triangulation is a tree, and a leaf is an ear: a triangle with two sides on the boundary. Remove the ear's tip, three-color the rest by induction, and give the tip the color that its two neighbors lack; this is a proper [graph coloring](c:graph-coloring).

steps.slogan: Choose the color class with the fewest vertices.
steps.detail: The three color classes partition the $n$ vertices. By the pigeonhole principle the smallest class has at most $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$ vertices.

steps.slogan: Show that guards at the chosen vertices see every triangle.
steps.detail: Each triangle has one vertex of each color, so it has a guard at a vertex. A triangle is convex, so that guard sees the whole triangle, and the triangles cover the polygon; so $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$ guards suffice.

steps.slogan: Show with comb polygons that $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$ guards are sometimes necessary.
steps.detail: A comb with $k$ narrow prongs has $n = 3k$ vertices, and no point sees into two prongs, so it needs $k$ guards; one or two extra base vertices give $n = 3k + 1$ and $3k + 2$. With step 4, $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$ is the exact worst case.

concepts.c:simple-polygon: Guarding is posed for simple polygons, which can be triangulated.
concepts.c:polygon-triangulation: The triangles are convex pieces that one guard sees completely.
concepts.c:graph-coloring: A three-coloring puts one vertex of each color in every triangle.

source.note: S. Fisk, A short proof of Chvátal's watchman theorem, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 24 (1978), 374; also in M. Aigner and G. M. Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $\chi$ the [character](c:character-of-a-representation) of a finite-dimensional complex representation of $G$. Then $\chi$ is a rational linear combination of characters $\operatorname{Ind}_C^G\psi$ [induced](c:induced-representation) from characters $\psi$ of [cyclic subgroups](c:cyclic-subgroup) $C$; more precisely, $|G|\chi$ is an integer combination of them.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
$\chi$ is the [character](c:character-of-a-representation) of a finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $\mathbb{C}$.

conclusion: $|G|\chi = \sum_C \operatorname{Ind}_C^G(\eta_C)$ over the cyclic subgroups $C$, with each $\eta_C$ an integer combination of irreducible characters of $C$, so $\chi$ is a rational combination of induced characters.

proofs.name: Serre's functions on cyclic subgroups
proofs.slogan: Write the constant $|G|$ as a sum of functions induced from cyclic subgroups, show that they are virtual characters, and multiply by $\chi$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the rational coefficients have denominators dividing $|G|$. The trivial group is the case $C = G$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the induction formula a finite sum and makes each element generate a finite cyclic subgroup.
The character $\chi$ is the factor that the projection formula moves inside each induced function.

steps.slogan: Define $\theta_A$ on each cyclic subgroup $A$ as $|A|$ on generators and $0$ elsewhere.
steps.detail: For a [cyclic subgroup](c:cyclic-subgroup) $A$, let $\theta_A(a) = |A|$ if $a$ generates $A$ and $\theta_A(a) = 0$ otherwise. Each $\theta_A$ is a [class function](c:class-function) on the abelian group $A$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\sum_A \operatorname{Ind}_A^G\theta_A$ is the constant function $|G|$.
steps.detail: The [induction](c:induced-representation) formula gives $\operatorname{Ind}_A^G\theta_A(x) = \#\{y \in G : y^{-1}xy \text{ generates } A\}$. Each $y \in G$ is counted for exactly one cyclic $A$, namely $\langle y^{-1}xy\rangle$, so the sum over all cyclic $A$ is $|G|$.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction on $|A|$ that $\theta_A$ is an integer combination of characters of $A$.
steps.detail: Step 2 for the group $A$ gives $|A| \cdot 1_A = \sum_{B \le A}\operatorname{Ind}_B^A\theta_B$. For $B \ne A$, $\theta_B$ lies in the [representation ring](c:representation-ring) $R(B)$ by induction, and induction maps $R(B)$ into $R(A)$, so $\theta_A = |A| \cdot 1_A - \sum_{B < A}\operatorname{Ind}_B^A\theta_B$ lies in $R(A)$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the identity of step 2 by $\chi$ and move $\chi$ inside each induction.
steps.detail: The projection formula $\operatorname{Ind}_A^G(\theta)\cdot\chi = \operatorname{Ind}_A^G(\theta\cdot\operatorname{Res}_A\chi)$ gives $|G|\chi = \sum_A \operatorname{Ind}_A^G(\theta_A\operatorname{Res}_A\chi)$. By step 3 each $\theta_A\operatorname{Res}_A\chi$ is an integer combination of irreducible characters of $A$, and dividing by $|G|$ gives the rational combination.

concepts.c:finite-group: Every element of a finite group generates a finite cyclic subgroup.
concepts.c:character-of-a-representation: The theorem expresses an arbitrary character through induced ones.
concepts.c:induced-representation: Induction from cyclic subgroups builds the spanning characters.
concepts.c:cyclic-subgroup: Cyclic subgroups carry the functions $\theta_A$ that sum to $|G|$.
concepts.c:class-function: The functions $\theta_A$ are class functions, not yet characters.
concepts.c:representation-ring: Step 3 places each $\theta_A$ in the ring of virtual characters.

source.note: The proof of Artin's theorem in J.-P. Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups, chapter 9.
